title: No. 48 — These Departments Should Not Be So Far Separated as to Have No Constitutional Control Over Each Other. (Madison)
paragraphs: The previous paper showed that the political maxim we examined does not require the legislative, executive, and judicial departments to be entirely disconnected from each other. Now I will show something further. Unless these departments are connected and blended enough to give each a constitutional check on the others, the separation that the maxim requires—essential to free government—can never in practice be properly maintained.

Everyone agrees that the powers belonging to one department should not be directly and fully exercised by either of the others. It is equally clear that none of them should hold, directly or indirectly, an overriding influence over the others in carrying out their respective powers. No one will deny that power tends to encroach, and that it must be effectively restrained from going beyond its assigned limits. After distinguishing in theory the several classes of power—legislative, executive, or judicial—the next and hardest task is to provide some practical security for each against invasion by the others. What this security should be is the great problem to be solved.

Will it be enough to mark out precisely the boundaries of these departments in the constitution and to trust those parchment barriers to hold back the encroaching spirit of power? This was the security relied on by the framers of most American constitutions. But experience tells us that this provision has been greatly overrated. Some stronger defense is absolutely necessary to protect the weaker members of government from the more powerful ones. The legislative department is everywhere extending the scope of its activity and pulling all power into its impetuous vortex.

The founders of our republics deserve so much credit for the wisdom they showed that pointing out their errors is an unpleasant task. But truth requires us to note this. They never seemed to take their eyes off one danger to liberty—the overgrown, all-grasping prerogative of a hereditary monarch supported by a hereditary branch of the legislature. They seem never to have remembered the danger from legislative usurpations, which, by gathering all power in the same hands, must lead to the same tyranny that executive usurpations threaten.

In a government where extensive prerogatives are placed in the hands of a hereditary monarch, the executive department is rightly seen as the source of danger. It is watched with all the jealousy that a zeal for liberty should inspire. In a democracy, where a multitude of people personally exercise legislative functions, they are continually exposed to ambitious intrigues from their executive officers. Their incapacity for regular deliberation and concerted action makes this worse, and tyranny may well arise on some favorable occasion from that quarter. But in a representative republic the executive office is carefully limited in both the extent and duration of its power. The legislative power is exercised by an assembly that, inspired by a supposed influence over the people, has fearless confidence in its own strength. It is numerous enough to feel all the passions that drive a multitude, yet not so numerous as to be incapable of pursuing those passions through reasonable means. It is against the enterprising ambition of this department that the people should direct all their jealousy and exhaust all their precautions.

The legislative department gains a superiority in our governments from other circumstances too. Its constitutional powers are at once more extensive and less open to precise limits. So it can more easily mask, under complicated and indirect measures, the encroachments it makes on the coordinate departments. In legislative bodies it is often a genuinely difficult question whether a particular measure will or will not extend beyond the legislative sphere. By contrast, executive power is restrained within a narrower compass and is simpler in nature, while the judiciary is marked by landmarks still less uncertain. Any attempt at usurpation by either of these departments would immediately reveal itself and fail. Nor is that all. The legislative department alone has access to the people's pockets. In some constitutions it has full discretion, and in all a prevailing influence, over the salaries of those who fill the other departments. This creates a dependence that gives still greater opportunity for legislative encroachments.

I have appealed to our own experience to confirm what I am saying. If proofs were needed, they could be multiplied endlessly. I could find a witness in every citizen who has taken part in or paid attention to the course of public affairs. I could gather records in abundance from the archives of every State in the Union. But for more concise and equally satisfactory evidence, I will point to the example of two States, attested by two unimpeachable authorities.

The first example is Virginia, a State which, as we have seen, has expressly declared in its constitution that the three great departments should not be intermixed. The authority in support of this is Mr. Jefferson, who, besides his other advantages for observing the operation of the government, was himself its chief magistrate. To convey fully the ideas his experience impressed on him, I must quote a substantial passage from his very interesting Notes on the State of Virginia, p. 195. "All the powers of government, legislative, executive, and judiciary, result to the legislative body. Concentrating these in the same hands is precisely the definition of despotic government. It will be no relief that these powers are exercised by many hands rather than one. One hundred and seventy-three despots would surely be as oppressive as one. Let those who doubt it look at the republic of Venice. Nor will it help us that they are chosen by ourselves. An ELECTIVE DESPOTISM was not the government we fought for. We fought for a government founded on free principles, in which the powers of government would be so divided and balanced among several bodies of magistracy that none could exceed their legal limits without being effectively checked and restrained by the others. For this reason, the convention that passed the ordinance of government laid its foundation on this basis: that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments should be separate and distinct, so that no person could exercise the powers of more than one of them at the same time. BUT NO BARRIER WAS PROVIDED BETWEEN THESE SEVERAL POWERS. The judiciary and the executive members were left dependent on the legislature for their salaries in office, and some of them for their continuance in it. If, therefore, the legislature assumes executive and judiciary powers, no opposition is likely to be made; nor, if made, can it be effective. In that case they may cast their proceedings into the form of acts of Assembly, which will render them binding on the other branches. They have accordingly, IN MANY instances, DECIDED RIGHTS that should have been left to JUDICIARY CONTROVERSY, and THE DIRECTION OF THE EXECUTIVE, DURING THE WHOLE TIME OF THEIR SESSION, IS BECOMING HABITUAL AND FAMILIAR."

The other State I will use as an example is Pennsylvania, and the other authority is the Council of Censors, which met in 1783 and 1784. Part of this body's duty, as set out in the constitution, was "to inquire whether the constitution had been preserved inviolate in every part; and whether the legislative and executive branches of government had performed their duty as guardians of the people, or assumed to themselves, or exercised, other or greater powers than they are entitled to by the constitution." In carrying out this trust, the council had to compare both the legislative and executive proceedings with the constitutional powers of these departments. From the facts they listed—most of which both sides in the council acknowledged—it appears that the constitution had been flagrantly violated by the legislature in many important instances.

A great number of laws had been passed that violated, without any apparent necessity, the rule requiring all bills of a public nature to be printed in advance for the people's consideration. This was one of the main precautions the constitution relied on against improper legislative acts.
The constitutional right to trial by jury had been violated, and powers had been assumed that the constitution had not delegated.

The salaries of judges, which the constitution expressly required to be fixed, had been varied from time to time. Cases belonging to the judiciary were frequently drawn into legislative cognizance and determination.

Anyone who wishes to see the specific items under each of these heads can consult the journals of the council, which are in print. Some of them, it will be found, may be attributable to peculiar circumstances connected with the war. But the greater part may be considered the spontaneous offshoots of an ill-constituted government.

It also appears that the executive department had not been innocent of frequent constitutional breaches. Three observations are in order here. FIRST, many of the instances were either directly produced by the necessities of the war or recommended by Congress or the commander-in-chief. SECOND, in most other instances, the executive conformed to either the declared or the known sentiments of the legislative department. THIRD, Pennsylvania's executive department is distinguished from those of the other States by the number of members composing it. In this respect, it has as much affinity to a legislative assembly as to an executive council. Being exempt from the restraint of individual responsibility for the body's acts, and drawing confidence from mutual example and joint influence, unauthorized measures would naturally be more freely hazarded than where the executive is administered by a single hand or by a few hands.

The conclusion I am justified in drawing from these observations is this. A mere parchment demarcation of the constitutional limits of the several departments is not a sufficient guard against the encroachments that lead to a tyrannical concentration of all the powers of government in the same hands.
